title: HashMap collision handling: chaining → treeify at threshold 8
keyPoints: A collision occurs when two different keys hash to the same bucket index (hash & (capacity - 1))
HashMap resolves collisions using chaining: multiple entries in the same bucket are stored as a linked list
Java 8+: when a bucket's chain reaches 8 nodes (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD) AND the table has at least 64 buckets, the chain converts to a Red-Black tree
Red-Black tree improves worst-case lookup from O(n) to O(log n) for collision-heavy buckets
When a tree shrinks to 6 or fewer nodes (UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD), it converts back to a linked list
With a good hashCode(), collisions follow a Poisson distribution; the probability of 8+ collisions in one bucket is about 0.00000006
Treeification is a safety net for bad hashCode implementations, not a feature to rely on; fix the hash function instead

s1_definition.oneliner: When two keys hash to the same bucket, HashMap chains them in a linked list; at 8 nodes the chain converts to a Red-Black tree (Java 8+) for O(log n) lookup instead of O(n).
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Collision**: two keys produce the same bucket index via `hash & (capacity - 1)`
- **Chaining**: colliding entries are stored as a linked list in the bucket; each Node holds hash, key, value, and a next pointer
- **Treeification** (Java 8+): when a chain reaches 8 nodes (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD) and the table has at least 64 buckets (MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY), the list converts to a Red-Black tree
- **Untreeification**: when a tree shrinks to 6 or fewer nodes (UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD), it converts back to a linked list
- A good hashCode() distributes keys evenly; treeification is a safety net, not the normal case
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a filing cabinet. Each drawer is a bucket. When two folders belong in the same drawer, you paper-clip them together in a chain (linked list). If 8 or more folders end up in one drawer, you replace the paper-clip chain with a sorted tab system (Red-Black tree) so you can find any folder by flipping to the right tab instead of scanning through all of them.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Hash collisions are inevitable because there are far more possible keys than buckets. HashMap handles them by chaining: colliding entries form a linked list in the same bucket. Before Java 8, a bad hash function could degrade HashMap to O(n) for every operation. Java 8 introduced treeification: when a chain reaches 8 nodes, it converts to a Red-Black tree, limiting the worst case to O(log n).

With a proper hash function, treeification almost never happens. The probability of 8 or more entries in one bucket is about 6 in 100 million. Treeification is a safety net, not a feature to rely on. If your HashMap is treeifying frequently, fix the hashCode() implementation.

In the National Bank of India system, Pankaj (the architect) discovered that a custom AccountKey class had a hashCode that returned the branch code – only 50 distinct values for 2 million accounts. This caused massive collisions and slow lookups. Fixing the hashCode to include accountId, branchCode, and accountType distributed entries evenly and eliminated the problem.

Remember one sentence: HashMap chains collisions in linked lists and converts to Red-Black trees at 8 nodes as a safety net, but the real fix is a good hashCode.
